stem:
Assume these statements are true:
1. If it rains on Monday, the flag ceremony is held in the gym.
2. It rains this Monday.

Which must be true?
choices: This Monday, the ceremony is held on the field.
This Monday, the ceremony is held in the gym.
This Monday, the ceremony is cancelled.
Next Monday, it will rain again.
answer: This Monday, the ceremony is held in the gym.
hints: Statement 1 is an if-then rule. Check whether its "if" part has happened.
The "if" part is "it rains on Monday". Statement 2 says it does rain this Monday.
When the "if" part of a rule is true, the "then" part must be true too. Read the "then" part of statement 1 and find the choice that matches it.

solution.methodName: Go forward, or flip and negate both parts

steps.action: Split statement 1 into its two parts. If-part: it rains on Monday. Then-part: the flag ceremony is held in the gym.
steps.why: An if-then rule says: whenever the if-part happens, the then-part happens.

steps.action: Statement 2 says the if-part happened: it rains this Monday.
So the then-part must happen: this Monday, the ceremony is held in the gym.
steps.why: This move is called modus ponens: if p then q; p is true; so q is true.

steps.action: "Held on the field" and "cancelled" both go against this, so they are false.
"Next Monday, it will rain again" is about a different day. Nothing in the statements tells us about next Monday.
The answer is "This Monday, the ceremony is held in the gym."

trapNotes.This Monday, the ceremony is held on the: The rule says that on a rainy Monday the ceremony is held in the gym. It cannot be on the field and in the gym at the same time, so this is false.
Nothing says the ceremony is cancelled. The rule says a rainy Monday moves it to the gym, so it is still held there.
The statements say nothing about next Monday. Counterexample: next Monday is sunny. Both statements stay true, but this choice is false.
